Topic 4.9 The Development of an American Culture, B. European Romanticism and American Culture

stimulus.text:
The table lists major works of the American Renaissance, the flowering of American literature in the early 1850s.

| Work | Author | Year |
|---|---|---|
| The Scarlet Letter | Nathaniel Hawthorne | 1850 |
| The House of the Seven Gables | Nathaniel Hawthorne | 1851 |
| Moby-Dick | Herman Melville | 1851 |
| Walden | Henry David Thoreau | 1854 |
| Leaves of Grass | Walt Whitman | 1855 |
stimulus.source_note: Table compiled from Barron's Premium 2027, Chapter 6, Topic 4.9 A, which names these five works as the peak of the American Renaissance in the early 1850s. Titles, authors, and years are as given in the book. Original synthesis, not a quotation.

source: original; stimulus as described in the stimulus source note
stem: The table best supports which conclusion about American literature by the 1850s?

options.text: American writers still depended entirely on British publishers
options.misconception: British books still sold in America, so it is easy to think nothing had changed.

options.text: No American writer had yet found a wide audience
options.misconception: These books are serious and demanding, so it is easy to think nobody read them.

options.text: Serious American literature of its own, beyond British books
American literature had turned away from American subjects
options.misconception: Melville sails far from America, so it is easy to think American subjects were left behind.

rationales.A: Five major books in five years, by four American authors, is the opposite of total dependence.
rationales.B: Cooper and Irving had already won wide audiences decades earlier, and these books followed them.
rationales.C: The table is a shelf of American classics, written in America about American questions, within a single half-decade.
rationales.D: Moby-Dick sails the world, but its captain, its ship, and its questions are American through and through.
rationales.general:
1. Count what the table shows. Five serious books, four American authors, five years.
2. Ask what that cluster means. A country that could fill a shelf like that in five years had its own literature.
Background: in 1800 American shelves were stocked with British authors; by the 1850s that had changed.
Remember: a cluster of dates can be an argument — five books in five years is a movement, not a coincidence.
